title: Operators & Expressions
description: Learn how C# performs calculations, comparisons, and logical operations. Complete every five-question quiz to unlock the next lesson and prepare for conditional statements.
completionText: You are ready for Module 4, where conditional statements guide program decisions using the operators you have mastered.

lessons.title: Introduction to Operators
objectives: Describe an expression as a statement producing a value.
theory: An operator is a symbol that performs an operation on one or more values. The values being operated on are called operands. Together, an operator and its operands form an expression.
In the expression 5 + 3, the plus sign is the operator and 5 and 3 are operands. This expression evaluates to 8.

Expressions are central to programming. They calculate new values, compare values, combine conditions, and drive programme logic. Every quiz answer, calculation, and decision depends on evaluating expressions.
C# has many operators: arithmetic operators for calculations, assignment operators for storing values, comparison operators for Boolean results, and logical operators for combining conditions.
Operators have precedence—some execute before others. Parentheses always execute first, making complex expressions clearer and less error-prone.
terms: A symbol performing an action on operands.
A value used by an operator.
The process of computing an expression's result.
lessons.tryIt: Write expressions adding two numbers, multiplying two variables, and combining three values with parentheses.
lessons.challenge: Create four variables and write three expressions mixing different operators and values.
mistakes: Do not confuse the operator symbol with variable names.
Remember that an expression must produce a value.
Use parentheses for clarity.
End statements with semicolons.
lessons.summary: An operator acts on operands to form an expression. Expressions evaluate to produce results that drive program logic.
quiz: An operator performs an action on operands.
The numbers being operated on are operands.
An expression combines operators and operands to produce a value.

lessons.title: Arithmetic Operators
objectives: Perform addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and modulus.
theory: Arithmetic operators act on numeric values. The plus operator + adds, minus - subtracts, asterisk * multiplies, forward slash / divides, and percent % computes the remainder.
When both operands are int, division produces an int result truncating any fractional part. (int)7 / 3 is 2. When either operand is double, division produces a double. 7.0 / 3 is 2.333...
The modulus operator returns the remainder. 17 % 5 is 2 because 17 divided by 5 is 3 with remainder 2. Modulus helps detect even and odd numbers: number % 2 == 0 means even.
Order of operations follows the PEMDAS/BODMAS rule: parentheses first, then multiplication and division from left to right, then addition and subtraction from left to right.
Expressions commonly represent real calculations. A game might compute damage as baseDamage * multiplier - armourReduction.
terms: The order in which operators execute.
lessons.tryIt: Calculate a recipe scaling, a game score penalty, and a remainder from a division.
lessons.challenge: Write a calculation for employee overtime pay, student average marks, and enemy health reduction.
mistakes: Integer division truncates without rounding.
Modulus works only with integers.
Order matters: 2 + 3 * 4 is 14, not 20.
Use parentheses to override precedence.
lessons.summary: Arithmetic operators calculate new values. Division behaves differently for int and double. Modulus finds remainders. Order of operations governs evaluation.
quiz: One double operand produces a double result.
The remainder of 17 divided by 5 is 2.

lessons.title: Assignment Operators
objectives: Recognise how compound operators simplify code.
Write clear and concise variable updates.
theory: The equals sign = is the basic assignment operator. It stores the right-hand value into the left-hand variable.
Compound assignment operators combine an arithmetic operator with assignment. score += 10 is equivalent to score = score + 10. The compound version is shorter and clearer.
Available compound operators are +=, -=, *=, /=, and %=. Each combines the corresponding arithmetic operator with assignment.
health -= 5 subtracts 5 from health. multiplier *= 2 doubles the multiplier. shares /= 4 divides shares by 4.
Using compound operators makes intent clearer and reduces the chance of accidentally typing the wrong variable name when updating a value.
terms: Storing a value in a variable.
lessons.tryIt: Create a variable and use four different compound assignment operators to modify it.
lessons.challenge: Build a score tracker using compound assignment for bonuses, penalties, and multipliers.
mistakes: Do not forget the variable name on the left side.
Remember that score += 5 is not the same as 5 += score.
Compound operators require a variable, not just a value.
Use appropriate suffixes for float and decimal.
lessons.summary: Assignment operators store values. Compound operators combine arithmetic with assignment, simplifying and clarifying code.
quiz: *= multiplies the variable by the right operand.
Compound operators are concise and readable.

lessons.title: Increment & Decrement Operators
theory: The increment operator ++ increases a variable by 1. The decrement operator -- decreases it by 1. These are shortcuts: score++ is equivalent to score += 1.
Prefix increment ++score increases the variable and then returns the new value. Postfix increment score++ increases the variable but returns the old value before the increase.
In most practical cases, prefix and postfix behave identically because the returned value is not used. int x = 5; x++; and ++x; both result in x being 6.
In loops and arrays, increment and decrement are essential. A loop counter increments each iteration. Countdown timers decrement. Practising with loops solidifies understanding.
Prefix is marginally more efficient in complex scenarios but both are suitable for beginners. The difference rarely matters in simple programs.
lessons.tryIt: Create a variable, increment it five times using ++, and display each result.
lessons.challenge: Build a countdown timer using decrement and a loop counter using increment.
mistakes: Prefix and postfix usually behave identically; do not overthink.
++ and -- require a variable, not a constant.
Use in loops where they are most common.
Avoid complex expressions mixing prefix, postfix, and other operators.
lessons.summary: Increment ++ adds 1; decrement -- subtracts 1. Prefix executes before returning; postfix after. Both simplify common updates.
quiz: Prefix vs postfix: Which increases first?
Both the same in most cases
Result of x++ in a simple statement?
The variable increases even if the returned value is ignored.
Both prefix and postfix are valid.

lessons.title: Comparison Operators
theory: Comparison operators test relationships between values and return a Boolean: true or false. They form the foundation of decision-making in programs.
The equals operator == tests whether two values are identical. 5 == 5 is true; 5 == 3 is false. The not-equals operator != is the opposite.
Less than < and greater than > compare magnitude. 3 < 5 is true. Less-than-or-equal <= and greater-than-or-equal >= include the boundary.
A common mistake is using = (assignment) instead of == (comparison). if (score = 10) assigns 10 to score and is syntactically different from if (score == 10).
Comparing strings with == checks reference equality, not content. Module 4 introduces proper string comparison. For now, focus on numeric comparisons.
lessons.tryIt: Create variables and test comparisons, printing the Boolean results.
lessons.challenge: Compare three numeric values and display whether each passes a threshold.
mistakes: Use == for comparison, = for assignment.
Remember that < and > do not include equality.
<= and >= include the boundary.
Numeric comparisons produce Boolean results.
lessons.summary: Comparison operators return true or false. They form the basis of conditional decisions and logic.

lessons.title: Logical Operators
theory: Logical operators combine Boolean values. The AND operator && returns true only when both operands are true. The OR operator || returns true when at least one operand is true. The NOT operator ! inverts a Boolean.
age >= 13 && age < 65 is true only if age satisfies both conditions. This range check is common for validation.
hasWeapon || hasShield is true if the player has either item or both. This allows flexibility in game logic.
!isGameOver flips the Boolean. If isGameOver is false, !isGameOver is true, making the game active.
C# uses short-circuit evaluation. In a && b, if a is false, b is never evaluated because the result must be false. In a || b, if a is true, b is skipped.
terms: At least one condition is true.
Skipping evaluation when result is certain.
lessons.tryIt: Write expressions combining three numeric comparisons with && and ||.
lessons.challenge: Build a game eligibility checker using multiple logical operators.
mistakes: Do not confuse && and || .
Remember that && is stricter than ||.
!true is false; !false is true.
Parentheses clarify complex logical expressions.
lessons.summary: Logical operators combine Booleans. && requires both true, || requires at least one true, ! inverts.
quiz: OR is false only when both operands are false.

lessons.title: Operator Precedence
theory: When an expression contains multiple operators, precedence determines which execute first. All operators have a precedence level established by C#.

Parentheses always execute first, making them the highest precedence. Then multiplication, division, and modulus from left to right. Then addition and subtraction from left to right. Then comparison operators. Then logical AND. Finally logical OR.
2 + 3 * 4 is 14, not 20, because * has higher precedence than +. Writing (2 + 3) * 4 makes intent explicit and produces 20.
Complex expressions become unreadable without parentheses. score >= 50 && bonus > 0 || lives > 0 is ambiguous. Rewrite as (score >= 50 && bonus > 0) || lives > 0 for clarity.
Readability is more important than relying on precedence memory. Break complex expressions into smaller parts or use intermediate variables.
lessons.tryIt: Write two expressions: one relying on precedence and one using parentheses for clarity.
lessons.challenge: Rewrite a complex expression using parentheses and break it into simpler intermediate calculations.
mistakes: Do not assume readers remember precedence rules.
Use parentheses liberally for clarity.
Precedence is left-to-right for same levels.
Test expressions by adding parentheses incrementally.
lessons.summary: Parentheses override precedence. Use them to clarify intent and make complex expressions readable.
quiz: AND has higher precedence than OR.

lessons.title: Practice Project · Student Grade Calculator
theory: This project integrates Module 3 concepts. It reads three assessment marks, calculates the average, identifies the highest and lowest values, and determines pass/fail status.
Use int or double for marks depending on whether decimals are allowed. Read three values using Console.ReadLine and Convert or TryParse.
Calculate average by adding marks and dividing by 3. Find the highest using comparison: if mark1 > mark2 && mark1 > mark3, mark1 is highest.
A student passes when average >= 50. Combine comparison and logical operators: average >= 50 && average >= 0.
Display all results using interpolation with labels and clear formatting. Use newlines and dashes to create visual structure.
lessons.tryIt: Build the calculator and test with three marks that produce a clear average and pass/fail result.
lessons.challenge: Add decimal support, calculate the lowest mark, and display additional statistics.
mistakes: Integer division truncates; use double for precise averages.
Validate that marks are within a valid range.
Ensure all three marks are read before calculating.
Check comparison logic for highest and lowest.
lessons.summary: You can now use arithmetic to calculate, comparisons to test conditions, and logical operators to combine them into complete programs.
quiz: How to find the highest of three values?
Operator for AND in the code?
Best data type for marks with decimals?
How to display pass or fail?
Both methods work; choose for clarity.
